14.1.crux: Some liquids conduct electricity and some don't; most conducting liquids are solutions of acids, bases or salts, which we can test with a simple tester.

cards.title: A simple tester
say: If the liquid conducts, the circuit is complete and the bulb glows.
If it doesn't, the bulb stays off.

cards.title: Why use an LED?

cols.head: Bulb
cells: May not glow for a weak current

cols.head: LED
cells: Glows even with a weak current

say: Some liquids conduct only a little. An LED can show even this small current.
A magnetic compass placed near the wire also deflects when current flows.

cards.title: Test results
say: Distilled water is pure, with no salts, so it hardly conducts.
Tap water has salts dissolved in it, so it conducts. Add salt to distilled water and it conducts too.
cards.remember: Acids, bases and salt solutions conduct electricity.

items.text: Never touch switches with wet hands
items.sub: Water can conduct electricity to you

crux_points: A tester (cell, bulb or LED, wires) shows whether a liquid conducts.
Acids, bases and salt solutions conduct electricity.
Distilled water hardly conducts; tap water conducts because of dissolved salts.

quiz.q: What is marked '?' in the tester?
quiz.why: The bulb or LED glows when current flows through the liquid.

quiz.q: Why does tap water conduct electricity but distilled water hardly does?
quiz.why: Dissolved salts make water a conductor.

14.2.crux: When current passes through a conducting solution it causes chemical changes: gas bubbles, metal deposits on the electrodes, or a change in colour.

cards.title: Chemical effects of current

items.sub: A layer forms on an electrode

say: The rods or plates dipped into the solution are called electrodes.
These changes are the chemical effects of electric current.

cards.title: Splitting water
say: In 1800, William Nicholson showed that current passing through water makes bubbles of oxygen and hydrogen.

cards.title: The potato test

steps.text: Push the two wires of a tester into a cut potato
A greenish-blue spot appears around the wire joined to the + terminal

say: This shows a chemical change, and helps find which terminal of a battery is positive.

crux_points: Current through a conducting solution causes chemical changes.
Signs: gas bubbles, metal deposits on electrodes, colour changes.
Water splits into oxygen (at +) and hydrogen (at –).

quiz.q: Which of these is a chemical effect of current?
quiz.why: Bubbles of gas show a chemical reaction caused by the current.

quiz.q: In a potato test, the greenish-blue spot appears near the wire joined to the…
quiz.why: The spot forms around the wire connected to the positive terminal.

14.3.crux: Electroplating uses electricity to coat a thin layer of one metal onto another, to make things shiny, rust-free or look costly.

cards.title: How electroplating works

labels.name: Object to be plated
labels.note: Joined to – terminal; gets coated with copper

say: Copper from the solution is deposited on the object joined to the negative terminal.
The same amount of copper dissolves from the plate at the positive terminal, so the solution stays the same.
cards.remember: The object to be coated goes on the NEGATIVE terminal.

cards.title: Where we see it

items.name: Chromium
items.eg: Bike handles, taps, car parts, gas burners: shiny, no rust, scratch-proof

items.name: Silver and gold
items.eg: Coated on cheaper metals for jewellery

items.name: Tin
items.eg: On iron food cans: food doesn't touch the iron

items.name: Zinc
items.eg: On iron in bridges and cars: protects from rust

say: Chromium is expensive, so objects are made of cheaper metal and only coated with chromium.

cards.title: A word of caution

steps.text: Used solutions can pollute water and soil
They must be disposed of following rules

say: Industry must handle these chemicals responsibly.

crux_points: Electroplating deposits a layer of metal on an object using electricity.
The object is joined to the negative terminal.
Uses: chromium on taps and bikes, tin on cans, zinc on iron, gold and silver on jewellery.

quiz.q: Which part is marked '?' in the electroplating set-up?
quiz.why: Metal from the solution deposits on the object joined to the negative terminal.

quiz.q: Why are food cans coated with tin?
options: Tin is less reactive, so food doesn't touch iron
quiz.why: Tin protects the food from reacting with the iron of the can.
